subject: statistics
title: Probability
summary: The rules of chance: sample spaces, complements, the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability, independence and Bayes' rule.

concepts.name: Sample space
concepts.summary: The sample space is the set of every possible outcome of a random process; an event is a set of outcomes, and its probability is a number from 0 to 1.

explain.text: The sample space is the list of everything that can happen when a random process runs once. Toss a coin twice and the sample space is HH, HT, TH and TT. An event is any set of those outcomes, such as "at least one head". Every probability is a number from 0, impossible, to 1, certain, and the probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1. When the outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it divided by the number in the sample space: three of the four outcomes have a head, so P(at least one head) = 3/4.

concepts.name: Complement rule
concepts.summary: The complement of an event A is everything in the sample space that is not in A, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

explain.text: The complement of an event A is everything that can happen except A. Either A happens or it does not, so the two probabilities add to 1, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A). If the chance of rain tomorrow is 0.3, the chance of no rain is 0.7. The rule earns its keep on "at least one" questions. The chance of at least one six in two rolls of a die has several cases, but its complement has one: no six either time, 5/6 × 5/6 = 25/36. So the answer is 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.

concepts.name: Addition rule
concepts.summary: The probability that A or B happens is P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); for mutually exclusive events the last term is 0.

explain.text: The addition rule gives the probability that at least one of two events happens: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Picture two overlapping circles in a Venn diagram. Adding the two circles counts the overlap twice, so it is taken away once. Draw one card from a deck: P(heart) is 13/52 and P(king) is 4/52, but the king of hearts is in both, so P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = 16/52. When two events cannot happen together, they are mutually exclusive, the overlap is empty, and the probabilities simply add.

concepts.name: Conditional probability
concepts.summary: The conditional probability P(A | B) is the chance of A once B is known to have happened: P(A and B) divided by P(B).

elements.name: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
P(A | B) is not P(B | A)

explain.text: A conditional probability is the chance of one event once you know another has happened. It is written P(A | B) and read "the probability of A given B". Knowing B shrinks the sample space to the outcomes in B, and you ask what share of those are also in A: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Roll a die and learn the result is even. Only 2, 4 and 6 are left, so P(six | even) = 1/3, not 1/6. Order matters: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are usually different numbers.

concepts.name: Multiplication rule
concepts.summary: The probability that A and B both happen is P(A) × P(B | A); a probability tree applies it by multiplying along each path.

elements.name: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A)

explain.text: The multiplication rule gives the probability that two things both happen: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A). The second factor is conditional because the first event can change the odds of the second. A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue marbles, and you take two without putting the first back. P(first red) is 3/5; then 2 red are left among 4, so P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. A probability tree lays this out: each branch carries a probability, and you multiply along a path to get the chance of that whole path.

concepts.name: Independent events
concepts.summary: Two events are independent when knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

explain.text: Two events are independent when knowing that one happened tells you nothing about the other: P(A | B) = P(A). Then the multiplication rule becomes P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), and checking that equation is the usual test. Tossing a coin and rolling a die are independent, so P(heads and a six) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. Independence is not the same as being mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so if one happens the other's chance drops to 0, which is a strong kind of dependence.

concepts.name: Bayes' rule
concepts.summary: Bayes' rule turns P(B | A) into P(A | B): P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B), where P(B) adds every path that leads to B.

explain.text: Bayes' rule reverses a conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B). It answers questions like "I tested positive, so how likely is it that I have the condition?" Suppose 1 in 10 people has a condition, the test is positive for 90% of them, and also positive for 10% of people without it. Positives come from two paths: 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.09 who have it and 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.09 who don't. Half of all positives have the condition, so the answer is 0.5, not 0.9. The starting rate, the prior, matters a great deal.

items.prompt: One fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability that it shows a number greater than 4?
items.explanation: Two of the six equally likely outcomes, 5 and 6, are greater than 4, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3. 1/6 counts only the 6; 4 itself is not greater than 4.

items.prompt: A coin is tossed twice. List its sample space.
items.answer: HH, HT, TH, TT: four equally likely outcomes.
items.explanation: Each toss can be heads or tails, and the order matters, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes. HT and TH are different outcomes.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
items.explanation: Of the four outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT, two (HT and TH) have exactly one head, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2. The answer 1/3 comes from treating 0, 1 and 2 heads as equally likely, but one head can happen two ways.

items.prompt: Which of these numbers cannot be a probability?
items.explanation: A probability is always between 0 and 1. 0 means impossible and 1 means certain, so both are allowed; 1.2 is more than certain, which cannot happen.

items.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that their sum is 7?
items.explanation: There are 36 equally likely pairs. Six give 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So the probability is 6/36 = 1/6. 1/11 treats the eleven sums 2 to 12 as equally likely, but they are not.

items.prompt: In probability, what is a set of outcomes, such as "the die shows an even number", called?
items.explanation: An outcome is one result of the process; an event is any collection of outcomes. "Even" is the event made of the outcomes 2, 4 and 6.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: A spinner can land on A, B or C. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(C)?
items.explanation: The probabilities of all the outcomes add to 1, so P(C) = 1 − 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2. 0.8 is P(A) + P(B), the chance of not landing on C.

items.prompt: The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability that it does not rain?
items.explanation: Rain and no rain are complements, so P(no rain) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

items.prompt: Write the complement rule for an event A.
items.explanation: Either A happens or it does not, and nothing else is possible, so P(A) + P(not A) = 1.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of at least one head?
items.explanation: The complement of at least one head is no heads, TTT, with probability 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. 3/8 is the chance of exactly one head.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to find the probability of at least one six in two rolls of a fair die.
steps: Write the complement: no six on either roll
items.explanation: The complement of at least one six is no six at all. Each roll misses six with probability 5/6, and the rolls are independent, so both miss with probability 25/36. The rest, 11/36, is the answer.

items.prompt: One die is rolled. Which pair of events are complements of each other?
choices: Even and odd
1 and 6
Less than 3 and greater than 3
Even and greater than 3
items.explanation: Complements cover every outcome with no overlap. Even (2, 4, 6) and odd (1, 3, 5) do. "Less than 3" and "greater than 3" leave out 3, and "even" and "greater than 3" share 4 and 6.

items.prompt: A student guesses on two multiple-choice questions, each with a 1/4 chance of being right, independently. What is the probability of getting at least one right?
items.explanation: Missing both has probability 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16, so at least one right is 1 − 9/16 = 7/16. Adding 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 counts the case of both right twice.

items.prompt: In the Venn diagram, the terracotta circle is event A and the blue-grey circle is event B. Tap the region of outcomes that are in A and in the complement of B.
items.explanation: The complement of B is everything outside the blue-grey circle. The part of A that lies outside B is the terracotta crescent, the part of A that does not overlap B.

items.prompt: In the Venn diagram, the terracotta circle is event A and the blue-grey circle is event B. Tap the region that is the complement of "A or B".
items.explanation: "A or B" is everything inside either circle. Its complement is what is left of the sample space outside both circles: the outcomes where neither A nor B happens.

items.prompt: Write the general addition rule for P(A or B).
items.answer: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
items.explanation: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the outcomes in both events twice, so P(A and B) is subtracted once.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a heart or a spade?
items.explanation: No card is both a heart and a spade, so the events are mutually exclusive and the probabilities add: 13/52 + 13/52 = 26/52 = 1/2. 1/16 multiplies them, which is the rule for "and", not "or".

items.prompt: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a heart or a king?
items.explanation: P(heart) = 13/52 and P(king) = 4/52, but the king of hearts is in both, so P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. 17/52 forgets to remove the card counted twice.

items.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. What is P(A or B)?
items.explanation: P(A or B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. 0.9 is the sum without taking off the overlap.

items.prompt: What are two events called when they cannot both happen on the same trial?
items.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so P(A and B) = 0 and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: In the Venn diagram, the terracotta circle is event A and the blue-grey circle is event B. Tap the region of outcomes where both A and B happen.
items.explanation: Outcomes in both events lie inside both circles, in the overlap. This is the region the addition rule subtracts once because P(A) and P(B) each count it.

items.prompt: In the Venn diagram, the terracotta circle is event A and the blue-grey circle is event B. Tap the region of outcomes that are in B but not in A.
items.explanation: These outcomes are inside the blue-grey circle but outside the terracotta one: the blue-grey crescent, not the overlap.

items.prompt: P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5. Which statement must be true?
choices: A and B are mutually exclusive
P(A and B) is at least 0.1
A and B are independent
P(A or B) = 1.1
items.explanation: P(A or B) can be at most 1, and P(A or B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − P(A and B), so P(A and B) is at least 0.1. They cannot be mutually exclusive, because then P(A or B) would be 1.1. Nothing given says whether they are independent.

items.prompt: Write the formula for P(A | B), the probability of A given B.
items.answer: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), where P(B) is not 0.
items.explanation: Knowing B happened limits attention to B's outcomes; the share of B that is also A is P(A and B) divided by P(B).

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: In a class of 40, 25 students play a sport, and 10 of those 25 also play an instrument. A sport player is picked at random. What is the probability they play an instrument?
items.explanation: Only the 25 sport players count, and 10 of them play an instrument, so the probability is 10/25 = 2/5. 1/4 is 10/40, which divides by the whole class instead of the sport players.

items.prompt: P(A and B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A | B)?
items.explanation: P(A | B) = 0.12 / 0.4 = 0.3. 0.048 multiplies the two numbers instead of dividing.

items.prompt: A fair die is rolled and you are told it shows an even number. What is the probability it shows 6?
items.explanation: Knowing the result is even leaves three equally likely outcomes, 2, 4 and 6, and one of them is 6, so the probability is 1/3. 1/6 ignores what you were told.

items.prompt: Of 100 people, 30 are left-handed and 20 play tennis. 6 people are left-handed tennis players. What is P(left-handed | plays tennis)?
items.explanation: Given tennis, only the 20 players count, and 6 of them are left-handed: 6/20 = 0.3. 0.2 is 6/30, which is P(plays tennis | left-handed), the condition the other way round.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to find P(A | B) from a two-way table of counts.
steps: Restrict attention to the outcomes in B
Count how many of those outcomes are also in A
Divide that count by the number of outcomes in B
items.explanation: Conditioning on B means B becomes the whole sample space. Within it, count the outcomes in A, then divide by B's total.

items.prompt: Write the general multiplication rule for P(A and B).
items.answer: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A).
items.explanation: The chance both happen is the chance A happens times the chance B happens once A has. It follows from rearranging P(B | A) = P(A and B) / P(A).

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
items.explanation: P(first red) = 3/5. Then 2 red remain among 4 marbles, so P(second red | first red) = 2/4. Both: 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10. 9/25 is 3/5 × 3/5, which would be right only with replacement.

items.prompt: A fair coin is tossed and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of heads and a 6?
items.explanation: The coin and the die do not affect each other, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. 2/3 adds 1/2 and 1/6, which is the wrong rule for "and".

items.prompt: 70% of commuters drive, and 20% of drivers arrive late. What proportion of all commuters are drivers who arrive late?
items.explanation: P(drive and late) = P(drive) × P(late | drive) = 0.7 × 0.2 = 0.14. 0.2 is the share of drivers who are late, not the share of all commuters.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to use a two-stage probability tree.
steps: Draw a branch for each outcome of the first event and write its probability
From the end of each first branch, draw the second event's branches with their conditional probabilities
Multiply along each path to get the probability of that pair of outcomes
Add the path probabilities that make up the event you want
items.explanation: The second stage hangs off the first, so its probabilities are conditional on the branch it grows from. Each path's probability is a product, and an event made of several paths is their sum.

items.prompt: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both are aces?
items.explanation: P(first ace) = 4/52. Then 3 aces remain among 51 cards. Both: 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221. 1/169 is (4/52)², which treats the draws as if the first card went back.

items.prompt: A and B are independent events. What is P(A | B) equal to?
items.explanation: Independence means learning that B happened does not change the chance of A, so the conditional probability equals the plain one.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?
choices: No, because P(A and B) is not 0
No, because P(A) is not equal to P(B)
Yes, because P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
Yes, because P(A) + P(B) is less than 1
items.explanation: 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2, which matches P(A and B), so they are independent. A nonzero overlap does not rule out independence; it rules out being mutually exclusive.

items.prompt: A and B are mutually exclusive, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. Are they independent?
choices: Yes, mutually exclusive events are always independent
No, because P(A and B) = 0 but P(A) × P(B) = 0.15
Yes, because they have no outcomes in common
Only if P(A or B) = 0.8
items.explanation: Mutually exclusive means P(A and B) = 0, but independence would need it to equal 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15. If A happens, B becomes impossible, so knowing one changes the other.

items.prompt: A fair coin has landed heads 5 times in a row. What is the probability that the next toss is heads?
choices: Less than 1/2, since tails is due
items.explanation: Tosses are independent: the coin has no memory, so the next toss is heads with probability 1/2. Believing tails is due is the gambler's fallacy. 1/64 is the chance of six heads in a row, judged before any toss.

items.prompt: Which pair of events is independent?
choices: Drawing a red card, then another red card, without replacement
Rolling a 6 on one die and a 6 on a second die
Being over 190 cm tall and playing professional basketball
Rain today and rain tomorrow in the same town
items.explanation: Two separate dice cannot affect each other. Without replacement, the first card changes what is left. Height and basketball are linked, and weather on one day tends to carry over to the next.

items.prompt: In a class of 20, 10 are girls and 8 wear glasses; 4 of the girls wear glasses. One student is picked at random. Are "girl" and "wears glasses" independent?
choices: No: 4 of the girls wear glasses, so the two events overlap
No: there are more girls in the class than glasses wearers
Yes: P(glasses | girl) = 4/10 = P(glasses)
Yes: exactly half of the class are girls
items.explanation: Among girls, 4/10 = 0.4 wear glasses, and in the whole class 8/20 = 0.4 do. Knowing the student is a girl does not change the chance, so the events are independent. Overlap alone says nothing about independence.

items.prompt: In Bayes' rule, what is the probability of a hypothesis before the evidence is taken into account called?
items.explanation: Bayes' rule updates the prior with the evidence to give the posterior probability.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: Write Bayes' rule for P(A | B) in terms of P(B | A).
items.answer: P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B).
items.explanation: Both P(A | B) × P(B) and P(B | A) × P(A) equal P(A and B); setting them equal and dividing by P(B) gives the rule.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

items.prompt: 1 in 10 people has a condition. A test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 10% of people who do not. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability they have the condition?
items.explanation: True positives: 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.09. False positives: 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.09. P(condition | positive) = 0.09 / (0.09 + 0.09) = 0.5. 0.9 is P(positive | condition), the conditional the other way round.

items.prompt: A tree's first branches are A and not A, and its second branches are B and not B. Put the steps in order to find P(A | B).
steps: Multiply along each path that ends in B
Add those path products to get P(B)
Divide the product on the A-then-B path by P(B)
items.explanation: P(B) is the total of every path that ends in B, the law of total probability. The share of that total coming through A is P(A | B).

items.prompt: P(A) = 0.4, P(B | A) = 0.5 and P(B | not A) = 0.25. What is P(B)?
items.explanation: P(B) = 0.4 × 0.5 + 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.35. 0.375 averages 0.5 and 0.25 without weighting them by P(A) = 0.4 and P(not A) = 0.6.

items.prompt: P(A) = 0.4, P(B | A) = 0.5 and P(B | not A) = 0.25. What is P(A | B)?
items.explanation: P(A and B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.2 + 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.35, so P(A | B) = 0.2 / 0.35 = 4/7. 1/2 is P(B | A), the reverse conditional.

items.prompt: What is the mistake called when someone judges P(A | B) while ignoring how rare A is to begin with?
items.answer: The base rate fallacy, also called base rate neglect.
items.explanation: Bayes' rule weights the evidence by the prior P(A). When A is rare, even fairly accurate evidence can leave P(A | B) low, and ignoring that is the base rate fallacy.

verification.note: Both solvers gave the same fact as the key, differing only in wording or notation.

artifacts.title: Two events in a sample space
artifacts.alt: A rectangle standing for the sample space holds two overlapping circles: a terracotta circle on the left for event A and a blue-grey circle on the right for event B. Their overlap is ochre, and the rest of the rectangle, outside both circles, is sage green.

artifacts.title: A probability tree for a medical test
artifacts.alt: A tree starts at a dot on the left. Its first branches lead to "Has it" with probability 0.1 and "Doesn't" with probability 0.9. From "Has it", branches lead to a positive result with probability 0.9, path total 0.09, and a negative with 0.1, total 0.01. From "Doesn't", branches lead to positive with 0.1, total 0.09, and negative with 0.9, total 0.81.

artifacts.title: Bayes' rule on a tree, step by step
artifacts.alt: Five steps over the medical test tree: the prior 0.1, the true positive path 0.09, the false positive path 0.09, their total 0.18, and the answer 0.09 / 0.18 = 0.5.

steps.title: Start with the prior
steps.text: 1 in 10 people has the condition, so P(has it) = 0.1 before any test.

steps.title: True positives
steps.text: 90% of people with the condition test positive: 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.09.

steps.title: False positives
steps.text: 10% of the 0.9 without it also test positive: 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.09.

steps.title: All positives
steps.text: Add the two paths that end in a positive: P(positive) = 0.09 + 0.09 = 0.18.

steps.title: The posterior
steps.text: P(has it | positive) = 0.09 / 0.18 = 0.5. Half of the positives have the condition.
